title: PRD: Structured payloads with progressive streaming, tool handoff, and deterministic error codes
creator: Asha Nair
description:
Summary: Define acceptance criteria and operational semantics for a versioned structured-output protocol that supports progressive/partial JSON streaming, explicit tool/function handoff signaling, deterministic error codes, and safe retry/idempotency semantics. Goal: enable SDKs and runtime to unambiguously parse, validate, and act on structured responses while preserving low-latency streaming, graceful degradation, and clear developer UX for error handling.

Scope: Protocol-level contract for model responses consumed by Redwood SDKs and platform tooling. Includes: message framing, schema negotiation, metadata frames (progress, confidence, provenance), tool-invocation envelope, handoff ACK/abort signals, error code taxonomy, and backpressure/retry rules. Excludes: model architecture changes, training-time behavior, third-party tool implementation details beyond invocation payload.

Success metrics: 1) SDKs parse 99.9% of production streaming responses without JSON deserialization errors; 2) Incidents caused by ambiguous tool-invocations reduced by 90% in first quarter post-release; 3) Parameterized automated regressions detect schema drift within 24 hours of model rollout.
acceptance_criteria: Protocol versioning: The response must include an explicit 'protocol_version' metadata field at the top-level stream handshake. SDKs and services must reject streams missing or with unsupported versions communicating a clear error frame.

Framing and streaming: Streaming responses must be emitted as a sequence of frames where each frame is either a 'delta' (partial JSON fragment), a 'meta' frame (progress, confidence, provenance), a 'tool-call' frame (invocation envelope), or an 'end' frame. SDKs must be able to reassemble deltas into valid JSON objects even if deltas split tokens or escape sequences occur across frames.

Partial JSON safety: The reassembly algorithm must tolerate split UTF-8 codepoints and incomplete escape sequences across frames; acceptance requires test harness with fuzzed split boundaries producing no parse exceptions in 10k simulated streams.

Deterministic error taxonomy: Define a fixed set of string error codes (e.g., PROTOCOL_VIOLATION, TOOL_UNAVAILABLE, TOOL_ERROR, SCHEMA_MISMATCH, INCOMPLETE_STREAM). Each frame may include an 'error_code' and 'human_message'. SDKs must surface both separately to callers for programmatic handling and user-facing messages.

Tool invocation envelope: A 'tool-call' frame must include 'tool_name', 'tool_version' (optional), 'call_id' (UUID), 'schema' (reference or inline), and 'args' (partial or full). Acceptance requires test vectors showing tool_call frames with inline and referenced schemas parsed and validated by the platform.

Handoff semantics: When the model emits a 'tool-call' frame the platform must: 1) persist call_id, 2) mark the request as awaiting tool response, and 3) accept an explicit 'tool-ack' or 'tool-abort' frame. If no 'tool-ack' arrives within a configurable timeout, the platform must emit TOOL_UNAVAILABLE. Acceptance requires integration tests simulating delayed ACKs and network partitions.

Idempotency and retries: Every tool-call must include a stable call_id deterministically derived from the logical request fingerprint and an optional nonce. Retries by client or platform for transient errors must be safe to replay if call_id is identical. Acceptance includes unit tests for duplicate-call detection and a failure-mode matrix documenting side effects for non-idempotent tool plugins.

Schema negotiation and validation: Consumers may reference a schema URL or inline JSON Schema draft-07. The platform must validate the final assembled JSON payload against the provided schema before marking a tool-call or response as complete. Acceptance requires negative test cases where schema violations produce SCHEMA_MISMATCH and are surfaced with failing fields list in human_message.

Streaming error propagation: If a mid-stream frame contains an unrecoverable protocol error, the platform must emit an 'end' frame with appropriate 'error_code' and a final partial diagnostic payload. SDKs must treat such streams as terminal and not attempt automatic reassembly beyond the end frame.

Backward compatible fallback: If a consumer does not support protocol_version >=2, the platform must provide a single-frame fallback representation (non-streamed) and set 'compatibility_fallback' meta flag. Acceptance includes end-to-end tests where older SDKs correctly receive fallback responses.

Observability hooks: Each stream must emit machine-readable trace attributes (request_id, call_id, model_id, protocol_version) to the console and traces. Acceptance requires a dashboard query that can filter by protocol_version and compute parse error rate within a sliding 1h window.

Performance SLOs: Streaming assembly must not add more than 10ms p95 CPU latency per request on dedicated runtime under normal load. Acceptance requires performance benchmark runs with released runtime configs and reporting of p50/p95/p99 overheads.

Security: Tool-call args may contain sensitive fields. The protocol must support an 'sensitive_fields' array of JSONPath expressions so platform masking and audit logs can redact. Acceptance requires that logs in the test environment do not contain unredacted values for declared sensitive fields.

Developer ergonomics: SDKs should expose a stable high-level helper that converts streaming frames into a single validated object or a tool invocation event stream. Acceptance requires integration tests for JS, Python, and Go SDKs using the helper APIs.

Compatibility matrix: Documented compatibility behavior for crossing model variants (quantized vs full) and routing fallbacks; acceptance requires simulated rollback where an older model variant emits older protocol version and platform triggers fallback behavior without request loss.
notes: Design trade-offs: We prefer an explicit frame type model (meta/delta/tool-call/end) to avoid brittle heuristics around JSON boundary detection. This increases payload verbosity but yields deterministic parsing.
We considered newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) but rejected it due to UTF-8 boundary fragility with model tokenization and streaming deltas.
Tool call id generation: default deterministic fingerprint algorithm will be sha256(request_text + user_id + route + timestamp_bucket) with a small optional nonce to force new calls when needed.
Fallback mode for very small responses will return a single 'end' frame with the entire payload and protocol_version provided to preserve compatibility for simple use-cases.
Edge case: if KV cache returns a cached prefix that itself contains a tool-call frame, runtime must preserve call_id and not generate new ones; acceptance tests must include cache-hit paths.
updates: 2025-02-19: Draft PRD posted; initial ENG/SDK review requested.
2025-02-25: Eng feedback: clarify framing encoding (binary vs utf8) and backpressure signaling; added performance SLOs.
2025-03-01: Design review: agreed on explicit 'tool-ack' and 'tool-abort' frames; requested sample SDK API surface for streaming helpers.
2025-03-03: Security reviewed masking approach; recommended explicit sensitive_fields and audit log redaction; security_review_required set to true.
estimated_risks: Parsing regressions if tokenizers change chunk boundaries — mitigate with fuzz harness and CI gating.
Operator confusion for aborted tool-calls — mitigate with clear observability and UI surfaces that show call_id and status.
Third-party tool side effects on duplicate calls — mitigate with recommended idempotency wrappers and clear docs.
